sources.entry: Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching - Measures branch-free search over sorted, Eytzinger and B-tree layouts, the winner changing with size and prefetch.

summary.title: Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching
summary.one_liner: Sorted order with binary search wins for small arrays, while the Eytzinger (BFS) layout is usually fastest for large arrays, contrary to earlier published results.
keywords: smallest value greater than or equal to x
takeaways: For small n, a sorted array with a well-implemented binary search is the best choice.
For large n, the Eytzinger (BFS) layout is usually the fastest in the authors' experiments, contrary to Brodal, Fagerberg, and Jacob (SODA 2003).
Eytzinger, implicit B-tree, and van Emde Boas layouts are compared against sorted order for finding the smallest value >= x.
The fastest C++ implementations use conditional moves to avoid branch mispredictions and prefetching to reduce cache latency.
summary.summary: This arXiv paper (Morin et al., v2 2017) studies how to order n comparable items in an array so that queries for the smallest value greater than or equal to x are fast when the array fits in RAM. It compares sorted order with binary search against the Eytzinger (BFS) layout, an implicit B-tree layout generalizing Eytzinger, and the van Emde Boas layout. The authors report extensive testing on varied modern hardware. They find sorted order best for small n and Eytzinger usually fastest for large n, and note their fastest C++ code uses conditional moves and prefetching.
